claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, during the week this post was published.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
In GeoDeploy's architecture, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math, but never makes judgment calls.
In GeoDeploy's architecture, Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use, but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names.
In GeoDeploy's architecture, Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS, but never decides anything.

GeoDeploy's request pipeline normalizes geos, enumerates region candidates using great-circle distance as a coverage measure, fetches live prices, bin-packs pods deterministically, has Jev decide the winning region and modules, composes a Pulumi program from a curated module registry, provisions via the Pulumi Automation API with one stack per region, and reports via plan.json/plan.md and a web UI.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
The Pulumi Automation API, as used by GeoDeploy, runs a preview and then an update, with one stack per region, and won't run at all unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.

GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules including EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
Jev does not return free text, but instead returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives: choice(), score(), and noul().
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence value.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric the caller describes, and GeoDeploy uses 10 levels for its rubrics.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.

Jev only ever selects from closed sets, choosing among region IDs GeoDeploy has already priced and checked, and never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates, along with the constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

In a single call, GeoDeploy asks Jev for a region selection, five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, and architecture consistency), two hard checks (data residency and capacity), and a fallback region choice.
TypeSafe's advice is to "describe situations, not degrees" when designing rubrics for its scoring primitive.

GeoDeploy's coverage rubric uses 10 levels ranging from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."
GeoDeploy's ranking system runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
GeoDeploy's latency-optimized weight profile uses weights cost:0.13, coverage:0.48, maturity:0.17, sprawl:0.1, archConsistency:0.12.
GeoDeploy's balanced weight profile uses weights cost:0.25, coverage:0.25, maturity:0.2, sprawl:0.12, archConsistency:0.18.
GeoDeploy's residency-first weight profile uses weights cost:0.12, coverage:0.12, maturity:0.38, sprawl:0.23, archConsistency:0.15.
GeoDeploy's failure-domain weight profile uses weights cost:0.08, coverage:0.17, maturity:0.48, sprawl:0.15, archConsistency:0.12.

In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), leaving Jev to decide only ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.
GeoDeploy gates the data-residency decision at a confidence threshold of 0.95, and hard-rejects if it doesn't pass.
GeoDeploy gates the region-for-a-new-cluster decision at a confidence threshold of 0.90, flagging the top three candidates for a human to choose if it doesn't pass.
GeoDeploy gates the region-when-a-stack-already-exists decision at a confidence threshold of 0.75, keeping the existing region if it doesn't pass.
GeoDeploy gates the ingress-or-autoscaling-module decision at a confidence threshold of 0.85, using the registry default if it doesn't pass.
GeoDeploy gates the node-pool sizing tier decision at a confidence threshold of 0.60, using the bin-packing result if it doesn't pass.
GeoDeploy applies a global floor confidence threshold of 0.50 for region pick, residency, or capacity decisions, dropping the AI path for that geo if it doesn't pass.

In GeoDeploy's engine.ts, the residency check is a hard gate that never soft-fails a compliance constraint, hard-rejecting below a confidence of 0.95 even rather than falling back to the model's own pick.
Each AiPathAborted error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so a rejected answer still ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
Running `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.

When self-driving mode is enabled via `geodeploy monitor`, the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, code (not Jev) computes the actual node-count changes.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, between 0.70 and 0.85 confidence the resize is suggested for a human to approve.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, below 0.70 confidence GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric, and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency or error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
GeoDeploy is released as open source, available at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The GeoDeploy project's source code is hosted at https://github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API documentation is located at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
TypeSafe Jev's documentation is located at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
The Pulumi Automation API is documented/linked at /automation/.
The options passed to choice() are the priced candidates themselves, keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
